summary: Proposes HighSpeed TCP, a change to TCP's congestion control for connections with large congestion windows. Standard TCP struggles to fill very fast, long paths. The RFC is experimental and notes that it is not a consensus that this is the best method for high-speed congestion control.

plainLanguage.summary: Normal TCP speeds up slowly after trouble, like climbing a hill one step at a time. On a huge fast highway that is too slow. This makes it climb quicker when the road is clearly big.

questions: tcp congestion control for high bandwidth
why is standard tcp slow on fast networks
what is the tcp response function
what is low_window in highspeed tcp
subtitle: An experimental tweak that lets TCP grow its window faster and back off less when paths are very fast.

tldr.problem: Standard TCP needs an unrealistically low packet loss rate to fill a very fast path. At 10 Gbps with 1500-byte packets and a 100 ms round-trip time, it would need an average window of 83,333 segments and at most one congestion event every 5,000,000,000 packets.
tldr.mechanism: HighSpeed TCP behaves exactly like Standard TCP while the congestion window is 38 segments or less. Above that, it increases the window by a(w) segments per round-trip time and cuts it by a factor b(w) after a loss, with both values read from a table.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Experimental and says it does not represent a consensus that this is the best method for high-speed congestion control. The authors encourage its use and ask for feedback.

today: RFC 3649 is an Experimental RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its abstract says it does not represent a consensus that this is the best method for high-speed congestion control.

sections.title: The Problem with Standard TCP at High Speed
sections.content:
In a steady state with packet loss rate p, Standard TCP's average congestion window is roughly 1.2/sqrt(p) segments. That function is the TCP response function: it maps the steady-state drop rate to the average sending rate in packets per round-trip time.

The consequence is harsh for fast paths. With 1500-byte packets and a 100 ms round-trip time, 10 Gbps needs an average window of 83,333 segments and a drop rate of at most 2*10^(-10), which the RFC calls an unrealistic requirement for current networks. The RFC's Table 1 shows the same pattern at lower speeds: 1 Gbps needs about 5555 round-trip times between losses.

People wanting 1 Gbps or more usually open several parallel connections or use MulTCP. The RFC says this leaves the number of connections to the user and is more aggressive in congested conditions, so it argues that a new approach is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard TCP only fills a very fast pipe if almost nothing ever goes wrong. That is like needing a perfectly empty road to drive fast. Real roads are never that clear.

sections.title: Design Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The design guidelines are to achieve high per-connection throughput without unrealistically low loss rates, to reach high throughput reasonably quickly in slow-start and when recovering from timeouts, and to need no extra feedback from routers or receivers. It must also be TCP-compatible in moderate or high congestion, such as packet drop rates of 1% or higher, so it adds no extra load there.

Three things are explicitly not goals: TCP-compatible performance at very low drop rates such as 10^-5 or 10^-6, ramping up faster than slow-start allows (which the authors believe needs explicit router feedback), and avoiding oscillations with one-way, long-lived flows that share the same large round-trip times.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is to go faster on huge empty roads without bullying other drivers on busy ones. It does not try to start faster from a standstill.

sections.title: The HighSpeed Response Function
sections.content:
The response function uses three parameters: Low_Window, High_Window and High_P. At or below Low_Window, HighSpeed TCP uses the Standard TCP response function. The RFC sets Low_Window to 38 segments, matching a drop rate of 10^-3, and sets High_Window to 83000 with High_P of 10^-7.

Keeping a straight line on a log-log scale gives the response function W = 0.12/p^0.835. A drop rate of 10^-7 then allows an average window of about 83,981 segments, against 3795 for Standard TCP. The RFC adds that this is roughly like N parallel TCP connections, where N(W) = 0.23*W^(0.4).

For the sender, the response function becomes two parameters. On each acknowledgement the window grows by w <- w + a(w)/w, and after a congestion event it shrinks by w <- (1-b(w))w. Standard TCP has a(w) = 1 and b(w) = 1/2. HighSpeed TCP uses the same values up to Low_Window, and sets b(w) to High_Decrease of 0.1 at 83000, which gives a(83000) = 72. The RFC expects implementations to use a pre-computed look-up table for a(w) and b(w).
sections.plainLanguage: Below a certain size, HighSpeed TCP acts like regular TCP. Above it, the bigger the window gets, the bigger the steps up and the smaller the step back after a stumble.

sections.title: Fairness and Trade-offs
sections.content:
Because HighSpeed TCP gets a larger window than Standard TCP at the same drop rate, it takes a bigger share of a shared link. The RFC's Table 5 shows relative fairness of 1.0 at drop rates of 10^-2 and 10^-3, 2.2 at 10^-4, 10.2 at 10^-6 and 22.1 at 10^-7. The authors judge that few connections operate in that regime today, so the benefits outweigh the unfairness, and they ask for feedback on this.

A new flow in congestion avoidance with a window of one packet also catches up much faster. After 1000 round-trip times, the HighSpeed window is 17409 packets while the Standard TCP window is 1000.

The cost is aggressiveness. At a window of 83,000 packets, HighSpeed TCP increases by 70 packets per round-trip time, which in a Drop-Tail queue can mean up to 70 drops in one loss event. The RFC says HighSpeed TCP and its variants place increased demands on queue management in routers.

The RFC also examines a linear alternative, W = 0.038/p, and Scalable TCP, which uses a fixed decrease of 1/8 and a fixed increase of 0.01 per acknowledgement. It judges the linear option less fair to Standard TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Taking bigger steps means HighSpeed TCP grabs a bigger slice of the road than regular TCP when both are driving. The authors think that is acceptable, but they ask others to check.

sections.title: Deployment Notes
sections.content:
HighSpeed TCP needs no change in routers or at the TCP receiver. It behaves exactly like Standard TCP whenever the congestion window is under 38 segments. Table 9 of the RFC gives the parameters for a 1500-byte, 100 ms path: at 10 Mbps a(w) is 1 and b(w) is 0.50, at 100 Mbps they are 6 and 0.35, and at 10 Gbps they are 70 and 0.10.

The effect is limited to connections whose receiver advertises a window of 118 MSS or larger. The RFC leaves short-term burstiness unspecified and suggests options such as rate-based pacing or maxburst, and it cautions against permanently reducing the window for that purpose. It also notes that with windows of 4MB or more, processing successive SACK packets after a drop becomes very time-consuming at the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the sending computer has to change. If the connection is small, nothing is different at all, so it is safe to try.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: the proposal makes no changes to the underlying security of TCP. The RFC has no IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: HighSpeed TCP does not add or remove any locks. It only changes how fast the sender speeds up.
